title: Means-ends_analysis
summary:
Means-ends analysis (MEA) is a problem-solving technique used commonly in artificial intelligence for limiting search in AI programs. It is also a technique used at least since the 1950s as a creativity tool. MEA is a heuristic problem-solving strategy in which an end goal is identified and then fulfilled via the generation of subgoals and action plans that help overcome obstacles encountered along the way.

The MEA technique is a strategy to control search in problem-solving. Given a current state and a goal state, an action is chosen which will reduce the difference between the two. For MEA to be effective, the goal-seeking system must have a means of associating to any kind of detectable difference those actions that are relevant to reducing that difference, and must also have means for detecting progress as some attempted sequences of actions may fail.

The idea of problem solving by means-ends analysis was introduced in 1972 by Allen Newell and Herbert A. Simon in their book Human Problem Solving. They developed the theory in the late 1950s and early 1960s while generating the General Problem Solver (GPS), a computer model capable of simulating human problem solving. GPS would recursively apply heuristic techniques and conduct a means-ends assessment after each subproblem was solved to determine whether it was closer to the intended solution.

Means-ends analysis is unique among problem-solving algorithms in that it emphasizes the generation of subgoals that directly contribute to reaching the end goal, with subgoals not necessarily of the same type. This differs from divide-and-conquer approaches where subproblems are always of the same type. Transformation problems, which require a sequence of operations on an initial state to reach a goal state, are best suited to MEA. Applications include AI systems, business planning and project management, and notable AI systems like Prodigy developed at Carnegie Mellon University.
